title: The Summer Burbn Was Cut Down to Photos, Comments and Likes
dek: In 2010 two worn-out founders threw away most of a year's work on a check-in app and kept the one part its few users loved.

story.event: Cutting the Burbn check-in app down to a photo-sharing app
story.summary: In 2010 Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger, with a $500,000 seed round behind their location app Burbn but only about a hundred users, decided to cut everything except photos, comments and likes. During a break in Mexico, Systrom made the first filter; about eight weeks after they sketched the new app, Instagram launched in October 2010 and, by Systrom's count, drew 25,000 sign-ups on its first day.
paragraphs: By the summer of 2010 Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger had a working iPhone version of Burbn, the app Systrom had begun at night while employed at a travel start-up in San Francisco. Burbn let people check in to places, make plans, earn points for time with friends and post photos. In March it had raised a $500,000 seed round from Baseline Ventures and Andreessen Horowitz.

The numbers were small. Systrom later put Burbn's users at about a hundred: "you can fit them in a room." Krieger recalled that active users were running flat while the pair kept telling themselves that more features or more speed would help. Foursquare and Gowalla already crowded the check-in space. But the people who stayed, Systrom said, loved the photos, and Krieger later said the keenest posters edited their pictures in other apps first.

They chose to cut. Writing on Quora, as TechCrunch reported, Systrom said the iPhone app "felt cluttered, and overrun with features" and that it was "really difficult to decide to start from scratch." They kept photos, comments and likes and dropped the rest. Krieger later said the change took a long time because some people loved Burbn, and many of those they would disappoint were friends and family. Their investors, by Systrom's account, told them to build whatever company they wanted from their ideas.

Both were worn out, Systrom said, so he took a break in Todos Santos, Mexico, with Nicole, now his wife, while Krieger built a prototype. On a beach walk she told him she would not post much, because her photos were not as good as a friend's who used filter apps. He went back to the room's dial-up connection, worked out a first filter, X-Pro II, and tested it on a photo of her foot and a stray dog near a taco stand.

About eight weeks after they sketched it, Instagram reached the App Store; TechCrunch reported its launch on 6 October 2010. Systrom said 25,000 people signed up on the first day, and its single server kept going down. Krieger said they went two days without sleep, "just devastated". The users came back anyway.

quote.text: The proceeding upon somewhat conceived in writing, doth for the most part facilitate dispatch: for though it should be wholly rejected, yet that negative is more pregnant of direction, than an indefinite; as ashes are more generative than dust.
quote.source_title: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Project Gutenberg eBook #575
quote.connection: Krieger later described Instagram as built on top of the ashes of Burbn. Bacon makes the same claim for any concrete draft: even when it is wholly rejected, a definite no gives more direction than a vague maybe. A year of Burbn told them what to keep.

reflection: Two things in this story are easy to miss. The hardest part of cutting Burbn was not technical; it was disappointing people the founders knew and liked. And the idea that made Instagram's first version work arrived during a break Systrom took because he was worn out.

You may be carrying something with more parts than anyone uses, some of them added because people you care about asked. You may also be telling yourself you cannot rest until it is fixed. Cutting back and stepping away can both be part of the work, not a retreat from it.
invitation: Ask one person who uses something you have built which single part they would miss if it disappeared. Spend your best hour today on that part alone, and leave the rest until tomorrow.

cross_checks.claim: Burbn raised a $500,000 seed round from Baseline Ventures and Andreessen Horowitz
Burbn had only about a hundred users, and the ones who stayed loved posting photos
The founders cut Burbn down to photo sharing, keeping photos, comments and likes
Instagram was built in about eight weeks after the decision
Disappointing existing Burbn users, many of them friends and family, made the change hard

research_notes: Launch date: TechCrunch reported the App Store launch on 6 October 2010; Systrom, interviewed by NPR in 2016, said 'We pressed launch on October 10 of 2010'. The story uses TechCrunch's contemporary date. Users: Systrom told NPR first that 80 or 90 people were using Burbn and then 'about 100'; the story says about a hundred. The first-day figure of 25,000 sign-ups is Systrom's own and is attributed to him; no independent contemporary count was found. Funding: TechCrunch (March 2010) reported a $500,000 seed round from Baseline Ventures and Andreessen Horowitz; Systrom told NPR that Steve Anderson's (Baseline's) initial $50,000 grew to $250,000 and Andreessen Horowitz added $250,000, consistent with the total. Timing of the decision: neither founder dates it precisely; TechCrunch says Instagram came 'just 8 weeks' after the restart and Systrom told NPR it was eight weeks from sketch to App Store, so the story places the decision in summer 2010. Krieger's remarks about disappointing friends and family and users 'running flat' come from South Park Commons's written notes of a 2019 talk, in his voice but possibly condensed, so the story paraphrases them rather than quoting. Systrom's Quora answer itself could not be loaded (Quora blocks automated requests), so his words are quoted from TechCrunch's reproduction. Nicole is named as in Systrom's NPR account; the friend 'Greg' is not named in the story. The connection's 'ashes' phrase is Krieger's, from the 92nd Street Y conversation published by Next Big Idea Club.
